query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase high-entropy alloy, toughness degradation at service conditions arises from a stress- and temperature-induced grain boundary complexion transition that is triggered by subtle, impurity-enhanced local compositional fluctuations. This complexion change reduces grain boundary cohesion and facilitates intergranular cracking, leading to brittle behavior even though classical intermetallic precipitates are absent.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy (for example, a well-annealed CoCrFeMnNi alloy) with a uniform grain structure and minimal intergranular precipitates.
generation.intervention: Subjecting the alloy to elevated temperature and mechanical loading that simulate service conditions, while deliberately introducing controlled levels of trace impurities (or comparing ultra-high-purity specimens with specimens containing low-level added oxygen or nitrogen) to encourage/complement the complexion transition.
generation.conditions: Tests performed at high service-relevant temperatures (e.g., 650–700°C) under cyclic or sustained mechanical loading conditions, with two sets of samples (ultra-high purity vs. controlled impurity addition).
generation.structural_mediator: The grain boundary state – specifically, a transition from a ductile, disordered boundary to an ordered, impurity-segregated complexion that acts as a brittle intergranular film.
generation.mechanism: Under high-temperature and high-strain conditions, even in a compositionally complex alloy, trace impurities or local chemical fluctuations can enrich at the grain boundaries. This enrichment triggers a complexion transition that reduces the cohesive strength of the boundaries without forming large intermetallic precipitates. The resulting localized loss in ductility initiates intergranular crack propagation, leading to overall brittle behavior. This mechanism contrasts with conventional alloys where toughness loss is driven by coarse grain-boundary precipitates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloy specimens with enhanced impurity content or induced complexion transitions will show a measurable reduction in toughness (e.g., lower fracture toughness and earlier crack initiation at grain boundaries) compared to ultra-high purity controls. In contrast, conventional alloys would exhibit brittleness predominantly due to coarser, brittle intermetallic precipitates.
generation.baseline: The toughness and ductility characteristics measured in the original, unaged, and impurity-minimized single-phase HEA.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be dominant in high-temperature, high-stress environments where even minute changes in grain boundary chemistry can be amplified. Its relevance may diminish under low-temperature or minimal loading conditions, and quantitative thresholds (e.g., critical impurity levels or specific complexion structures) remain uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The exact impurity concentration that triggers the complexion transition, the kinetics of segregation under service conditions, and the interplay with grain size or other microstructural features are not fully defined and require further quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the same single-phase HEA: one using ultra-high-purity processing and the other with a controlled addition of known trace impurities (e.g., oxygen or nitrogen). Subject both batches to identical thermal aging (e.g., 700°C for various durations) and mechanical loading protocols. Use high-resolution characterization methods (such as atom probe tomography and transmission electron microscopy) to analyze grain boundary composition and structure, and perform fracture toughness tests to evaluate their mechanical response.
measurements: Grain boundary chemical composition (via atom probe or high-resolution EDS)
Grain boundary morphology and possible complexion state (via TEM or STEM)
Fracture toughness and crack initiation/propagation behavior
Comparison of mechanical performance (ductility, toughness) under cyclic loading
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant difference in grain boundary composition or structure is detected between the two batches and both exhibit similar toughness characteristics, then the proposed mechanism—i.e., that a complexion transition mediated by impurity segregation reduces toughness—is falsified.

Origin of age softening in the refractory high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are emerging materials with potential for use under extreme conditions. As a newly developed material system, a comprehensive understanding of their long-term stability under potential service temperatures remains to be established. This study examined a titanium-vanadium-niobium-tantalum alloy, a promising RHEA known for its superior high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility. Using a combination of advanced analytical microscopies, Calculation of Phase Diagrams (CALPHAD) software, and nanoindentation, we investigated the evolution of its microstructure and mechanical properties upon aging at 700°C. Trace interstitials such as oxygen and nitrogen, initially contributing to solid solution strengthening, promote phase segregation during thermal aging. As a result of the depletion of solute interstitials within the metal matrix, a progressive softening is observed in the alloy as a function of aging time. Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). Effect of serrated grain boundary on tensile and creep properties of a precipitation strengthened high entropy alloy

Abstract: ABSTRACTIn this study, tensile and creep deformation of a high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) has been investigated; hot ductility drop was identified at first, and the loss of ductility at elevated temperature was associated with intergranular fracture. By modifying the grain boundary morphology from straight to serration, the hot ductility drop issue has been resolved successfully. The serrated grain boundary could be achieved by reducing the cooling rate of solution heat treatment, which allowed the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates to interfere with mobile grain boundaries, resulting in undulation of the grain boundary morphology. Tensile and creep tests at 650°C were conducted, and serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively.
